data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A large service with internal redundancy is fundamentally more fragile than a decentralized network because it creates a 'Single Point of Coordination' that enables instantaneous global failure.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The decentralized network uses a shared automated update mechanism or a common upstream dependency (e.g., a single NPM package used by all).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The failure is caused by an external surge in demand (DDoS) that overwhelms all services regardless of their coordination.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Centralized systems rely on unified control planes for efficiency (e.g., global config pushes, synchronized updates). This coordination mechanism acts as a high-speed vector for correlated failure: a single erroneous 'global' command can disable all redundant nodes simultaneously. In contrast, a decentralized network requires asynchronous, manual, or independent updates across operators, which naturally 'staggers' the propagation of errors, transforming a potential global outage into a series of manageable, localized failures.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
